quotes.t: The bulk of the world's knowledge is an imaginary construction.
Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. The fearful are caught as often as the bold.
Be not dumb, obedient slaves in an army of destruction. Be heroes in an army of construction.
There is timing in everything. Timing in strategy cannot be mastered without a great deal of practice.
The Way of strategy is the Way of nature. When you appreciate the power of nature, knowing the rhythm of any situation, you will be able to hit the enemy naturally and strike naturally.
In strategy your spiritual bearing must not be any different from normal. Both in fighting and in everyday life you should be determined though calm.
Management of many is the same as management of few. It is a matter of organization.
Treat your men as you would your own beloved sons. And they will follow you into the deepest valley.
Speed is the essence of war. Take advantage of the enemy's unpreparedness; travel by unexpected routes and strike him where he has taken no precautions.
To succeed, you must have tremendous perseverance, tremendous will.
The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength.
quotes.source: Vivekananda: His Call to the Nation

quotes.t: Faith, faith, faith in ourselves, faith, faith in God, this is the secret of greatness.
quotes.source: Vivekananda: His Call to the Nation

quotes.t: Whoever in discussion adduces authority uses not intellect but rather memory.
Life well spent is long.
Human subtlety will never devise an invention more beautiful, more simple or more direct than does nature, because in her inventions nothing is lacking, and nothing is superfluous.
Total commitment is the common denominator among all successful men and women.
The best way to win was to not need to win. The best performances are accomplished when you are relaxed and free of doubt.
To live only for some unknown future is superficial. It is like climbing a mountain to reach the peak without experiencing its sides.
What other people label or might try to call failure, I have learned is just God's way of pointing you in a new direction.
You are not your circumstances. You are your possibilities. If you know that, you can do anything.
Nourish what makes you feel confident, connected, contented. Opportunity will rise to meet you.
It takes courage to love, but pain through love is the purifying fire which those who love generously know.
I think, at a child's birth, if a mother could ask a fairy godmother to endow it with the most useful gift, that gift should be curiosity.
quotes.source: In Defense of Curiosity, Saturday Evening Post (1935)

quotes.t: Freedom makes a huge requirement of every human being. With freedom comes responsibility.
Experience is the child of Thought, and Thought is the child of Action. We can not learn men from books.
Next to knowing when to seize an opportunity, the most important thing in life is to know when to forego an advantage.
Grief is the agony of an instant; the indulgence of Grief the blunder of a life.
Art is the supreme task and the truly metaphysical activity in this life.
Here the ways of men part: if you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.
A witticism is an epigram on the death of a feeling.
Only free men can negotiate; prisoners cannot enter into contracts. Your freedom and mine cannot be separated.
quotes.source: Refusing to bargain for freedom, as quoted in TIME (25 February 1985)

quotes.t: Our march to freedom is irreversible. We must not allow fear to stand in our way.
quotes.source: Our March to Freedom is Irreversible (1990)

quotes.t: They recognised that an injury to one is an injury to all and therefore acted together in defense of justice and a common human decency.
quotes.source: Nobel Peace Prize acceptance speech (10 December 1993)

quotes.t: To make light of philosophy is to be a true philosopher.
People almost invariably arrive at their beliefs not on the basis of proof but on the basis of what they find attractive.
It is a natural illness of man to think that he possesses the truth directly.
Art is not made to decorate rooms. It is an offensive and defensive weapon against the enemy.
It isn't up to the painter to define the symbols.
quotes.source: Reply on the symbolism of Guernica (1937)

quotes.t: To me there is no past or future in my art. If a work of art cannot live always in the present it must not be considered at all.
Love is a fruit in season at all times, and within reach of every hand.
quotes.source: Love, A Fruit Always in Season (1987)

quotes.t: We are called upon not to be successful, but to be faithful.
quotes.source: To Navin Chawla, her authorized biographer

quotes.t: Be kind to each other in your homes. Be kind to those who surround you. I prefer that you make mistakes in kindness rather than that you work miracles in unkindness.
quotes.source: Mother Teresa: Her Mission to Serve God by Caring for the Poor (1988)

quotes.t: A day will come when there will be no battlefields, but markets opening to commerce and minds opening to ideas.
quotes.source: Opening address, Peace Congress, Paris (21 August 1849)

quotes.t: One can no more pray too much than love too much.
Happy, even in anguish, is he to whom God has given a soul worthy of love and of grief!
The realization that life is absurd cannot be an end, but only a beginning.
quotes.source: Review of Nausea, Alger Républicain (20 October 1938)

quotes.t: We always deceive ourselves twice about the people we love — first to their advantage, then to their disadvantage.
Man cannot do without beauty, and this is what our era pretends to want to disregard.
We're more popular than Jesus now; I don't know which will go first — rock and roll or Christianity.
Will the people in the cheaper seats clap your hands? All the rest of you, if you'll just rattle your jewellery.
When I cannot sing my heart, I can only speak my mind.
The golden rule is that there are no golden rules.
Men are wise in proportion, not to their experience, but to their capacity for experience.
Happiness and beauty are by-products.
For kindness is ever the begetter of kindness.
In knowing nothing is the sweetest life.
Fear? What has a man to do with fear? Chance rules our lives, and the future is all unknown. Best live as we may, from day to day.
Any religion or philosophy which is not based on a respect for life is not a true religion or philosophy.
quotes.source: Letter to a Japanese Animal Welfare Society (1961)

quotes.t: It is good to maintain and further life — it is bad to damage and destroy life.
quotes.source: Quoted in Albert Schweitzer: The Man and His Mind (1947)

quotes.t: Truth has no special time of its own. Its hour is now — always, and indeed then most truly when it seems most unsuitable to actual circumstances.
quotes.source: On the Edge of the Primeval Forest

quotes.t: From the heights of these pyramids, forty centuries look down on us.
quotes.source: Speech to his troops in Egypt (21 July 1798)

quotes.t: Letting there be room for not knowing is the most important thing of all.
No one knows whether death may not be the greatest of all blessings for a man, yet men fear it as if they knew that it is the greatest of evils.
He who asks a question is a fool for five minutes; he who does not ask a question remains a fool forever.
I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude.
Students, when you want to say something, think about it three times before you say it. Speak only if your words will benefit yourselves and others. Do not speak if it brings no benefit.
Crises and deadlocks when they occur have at least this advantage, that they force us to think.
quotes.source: The Unity of India: Collected Writings, 1937-1940 (1942)

quotes.t: Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
Love truth, but pardon error.
quotes.source: Sept Discours en Vers sur l'Homme (1738)

quotes.t: Let no man pull you so low as to hate him.
Much Madness is divinest Sense
quotes.source: Much Madness is divinest Sense (Johnson no. 435)

quotes.t: I wear the chain I forged in life.
Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.
To be fond of dancing was a certain step towards falling in love.
The vocation of every man and woman is to serve other people.
The wisest of all, in my opinion, is he who can, if only once a month, call himself a fool — a faculty unheard of nowadays.
I've learned one thing: you only really get to know a person after a fight. Only then can you judge their true character!
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: I am not interested in picking up crumbs of compassion thrown from the table of someone who considers himself my master. I want the full menu of rights.
You cannot save people, you can only love them.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Volume Two (1934-1939)

quotes.t: A good reputation is more valuable than money.
The weakest living creature, by concentrating his powers on a single object, can accomplish something.
The eyes of others our prisons; their thoughts our cages.
Have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become.
I will revenge my injuries: if I cannot inspire love, I will cause fear; and chiefly towards you my arch-enemy, because my creator, do I swear inextinguishable hatred.
Do you not see how necessary a world of pains and troubles is to school an intelligence and make it a soul?
quotes.source: Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 1819

quotes.t: There is no hurry. We shall get there some day.
The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
Love, n. A temporary insanity curable by marriage or by removal of the patient from the influences under which he incurred the disorder.
If we had no winter, the spring would not be so pleasant.
It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.
A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the truth.
Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
quotes.source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792)

quotes.t: I love myself when I am laughing, and then again when I am looking mean and impressive.
My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
Literature is news that stays news.
I may sometimes be willing to teach for nothing, but if paid at all, I shall never do a man's work for less than a man's pay.
If we winter this one out, we can summer anywhere.
The white man's happiness cannot be purchased by the black man's misery.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845)

quotes.t: Be joyful though you have considered all the facts.
quotes.source: Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front (1970)

A. A. Milne.bio: A. A. Milne was an English author best known for the Winnie-the-Pooh stories, created for his son Christopher Robin and inspired by his stuffed animals. A successful playwright and humourist before Pooh, he also wrote the classic children's poems of When We Were Very Young.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Ada Lovelace.bio: English mathematician (1815–1852), who wrote the first algorithm intended to be processed by a machine.

Aesop.bio: Aesop was a storyteller of ancient Greece, traditionally said to have been an enslaved man who won freedom through his wit. The animal fables credited to him, such as The Tortoise and the Hare, have taught moral lessons for over two millennia.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Ambrose Bierce.bio: American short-story writer, satirist and Civil War veteran, author of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge and The Devil's Dictionary (1906). He disappeared in Mexico in 1914 while observing the revolution.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Bradstreet.bio: English-born colonial American poet and the first writer from Britain's North American colonies to be published. Her collection The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America appeared in 1650.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Arthur Conan Doyle.bio: Scottish writer, creator of Sherlock Holmes.
Arthur Conan Doyle.credit: The Library of Congress, Public domain

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Clara Barton.bio: American nurse (1821-1912) who founded the American Red Cross in 1881.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Ezra Pound.bio: American poet and critic (1885-1972), a major figure of Modernism.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Langston Hughes.bio: American poet and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Mary Wollstonecraft.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and advocate of women's rights, best known for A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). She argued that women are not naturally inferior to men but appear so because of a lack of education. She was the mother of Frankenstein author Mary Shelley.

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Seamus Heaney.bio: Irish poet (1939-2013) who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1995.

Simone de Beauvoir.bio: French writer and existentialist philosopher, author of The Second Sex.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Zora Neale Hurston.bio: Zora Neale Hurston was an American writer and anthropologist at the heart of the Harlem Renaissance, celebrated for her novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Trained under Franz Boas, she documented the folklore, music and speech of the rural Black South.
